detail.title: A Case study Disrupting the Duopoly: How Transsion Holdings Challenged Established Brands in the Philippines
detail.abstract: This case study examines the strategic management and market placement of Transsion Holdings in the Philippines, specifically through its multi-brand portfolio: itel, Infinix, and Tecno. As of 2024, Transsion has secured a dominant position in the local smartphone industry by prioritizing affordability, localized feature sets, and aggressive distribution networks. By applying a "Think Globally, Act Locally" framework, Transsion effectively navigates the competitive landscape dominated by established players like Samsung and Xiaomi. This study analyzes how Transsion’s branding—focusing on the sub-₱11,500 price segment and performance-driven hardware—shapes consumer purchase behavior and brand loyalty in the Philippine market. The findings suggest that Transsion’s success is a result of a highly segmented product matrix and a deep understanding of the local "Shopertainment" and gaming-centric consumer culture.

title: The New Era of Marketing: A Case Study on Hindustan Unilever Limited (HUL) FMCG in India

detail.title: The New Era of Marketing: A Case Study on Hindustan Unilever Limited (HUL) FMCG in India
detail.abstract: The Indian Fast-Moving Consumer Goods (FMCG) market is undergoing a seismic shift, This paper explores the "new era of marketing" in the Indian FMCG sector, particularly highlighting Hindustan Unilever Limited (HUL), a key industry leader. The shift is influenced by various elements, including greater internet accessibility, changing consumer behaviours, and the rise of digital platforms. We analyse how HUL is adapting its marketing strategies to navigate these changes, encompassing areas like digital marketing, personalized consumer engagement, sustainable brand building, and the integration of data analytics. Through a case study approach, this paper explores HUL's initiatives, their successes, and the challenges they face in maintaining market leadership in this dynamic environment. The findings offer insights into the broader trends shaping marketing practices in the Indian FMCG sector and highlight the importance of agility, innovation, and consumer-centricity in the current landscape.

title: Learning Correlated Preferences via Inverse Optimization: Applications to Bundle Pricing
affiliations: Shanghai Jiao Tong University (SJTU) - Antai College of Economics and Management

detail.title: Learning Correlated Preferences via Inverse Optimization: Applications to Bundle Pricing
detail.abstract: We study how to learn correlated preferences from aggregate choice data through inverse optimization. Our focus is the Cross-Moment Model (CMM), a representative-agent choice model that captures rich substitution patterns via first two moments while remaining tractable for downstream optimization problems such as bundle pricing. Despite these attractive properties, CMM has seen limited empirical use because estimation requires recovering a latent covariance matrix from market shares. We propose a suboptimality-loss framework for CMM estimation. Instead of matching probabilities directly, we measure how suboptimal the observed shares are for the forward CMM problem induced by candidate parameters. We show that this loss is convex in the utility coefficients and admits a difference-of-convex representation in the covariance matrix. Leveraging this structure, we develop an alternating algorithm that combines projected-gradient updates for the utility block with a majorization-minimization step for the covariance block. The resulting covariance subproblem is convex, and the projection onto the feasible covariance set admits a closed-form spectral formula. We establish descent and sublinear stationarity guarantees for the proposed scheme. On the statistical side, we provide a local loss-based identification result in the noiseless correctly specified setting, supported by a local secondorder analysis of the population loss, and a finite-sample guarantee for market-share prediction when observed shares are empirical frequencies. Numerical experiments show stable convergence under correct specification, strong predictive performance under misspecification, and meaningful pricing gains in a synthetic bundling setting where correlation matters.

title: Social Systems of Innovation and Production at the National Level? A closer look at the Sectoral Political Economic Dynamics of the British and Japanese Large Commercial Aircraft Industries.

detail.title: Social Systems of Innovation and Production at the National Level? A closer look at the Sectoral Political Economic Dynamics of the British and Japanese Large Commercial Aircraft Industries.

keywords: Social Systems of Innovation and Production

detail.abstract:
This 103-page Master thesis examines whether innovation and production in the large commercial aircraft industry align with national-level social systems, as posited by Varieties of Capitalism (VoC) and National Systems of Innovation (NIS) frameworks, or if sectoral political economic dynamics prevail. Contrasting Britain's Liberal Market Economy (LME)—characterized by market-driven relations, short-term orientation, and radical innovation—with Japan's Coordinated Market Economy (CME)—marked by inter-firm networks, long-term stability, and incremental improvements—the study analyzes the British and Japanese aircraft sectors as units of analysis.

Three sub-questions guide the inquiry: (1) To what extent do features and dynamics of the commercial aircraft industry converge or diverge between the UK and Japan? (2) Is there a mismatch between sectoral requirements (e.g., governance, R&D, inter-firm relations) and national institutional capabilities? (3) In cases of mismatch, do patterns emerge of subordinate systems (voluntaristic deviations) or sub-sectoral specialization (path-dependent adaptation)?

Employing a neo-institutionalist lens, the analysis benchmarks "universal" sectoral standards from leading aircraft producers against UK and Japanese institutional patterns (Chapters 3-4). Findings challenge rigid national determinism, revealing hybrid sectoral dynamics that temper VoC/NIS predictions while still acknowledging the prevalence of the impact of National Innovation Systems on the competitive trajectory and performance of the wide-body aircraft manufacturing industries of Japan and Great Britain. Implications refine debates on institutional fit, path dependency, and sectoral autonomy in complex high-tech industries.

title: The Role of Ethics, Morality, and Sustainability in Shaping Consumer Decision-Making in the Fashion and Beauty Retail Industries

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: All survey participants provided informed consent prior to participation. No personally identifiable information was collected. Interview participants consented to the use of anonymized quotations from their responses.

detail.abstract:
This thesis explores the role of ethics, morality, and sustainability in shaping consumer decision-making within the fashion and beauty industries. It investigates the tension between what consumers say they believe and what they actually do, uncovering the drivers behind the value-action gap that continues to challenge ethical and sustainable retail efforts. By combining quantitative survey data with demographic segmentation and qualitative analysis, this study provides an in-depth look at how consumer behavior is influenced not just by values, but by access, privilege, and social context.

The research demonstrates that factors such as income, education, geography, etc., play a significant role in determining how consumers perceive ethicality and sustainability - and more importantly, whether they feel empowered to act on those beliefs. While consumers with higher socioeconomic status were more likely to report alignment with ethical values, this appeared more a reflection of flexibility and convenience than deeper morality. Conversely, lower-income consumers often shared similar ideals but lacked the financial or logistical means to act in line with them, highlighting the systemic nature of ethical consumption.

The thesis introduces the Strategic Sustainability Integration Model (SSIM), a practical framework designed to help brands embed ethical principles into their business without placing the burden of responsibility solely on the consumer. The model accounts for factors such as brand transparency, ease of access, pricing strategy, and cultural alignment - showing how businesses can strategically lower the barriers to sustainable purchasing.

This research challenges the traditional narrative that ethical consumption is simply a matter of individual choice. Instead, it reframes it as a complex interaction between moral intention, structural limitations, and commercial design. The findings offer practical recommendations for luxury, fast fashion, and beauty brands - particularly in the MENA region - seeking to create more inclusive and sustainable consumer pathways. By understanding and addressing the real reasons why consumers fall short of their values, brands can design better systems, build stronger loyalty, and drive more meaningful changes in the industry.

detail.abstract: The present research is a bibliometric study of scholarly publications on the topic of viral marketing that was published in 2020-2025, a time marked by an accelerated technological advancement and a societal upheaval. Biblioshiny, a module in Bibliometrix R package, was used to conduct an examination of corpus of 269 publications in 139 journals. The research questions are explored on the basis of publication patterns, coauthorship patterns, patterns of key word co-occurrence, and institutional productivity. Results indicate steady increases in the number of publications with sharp increases in 2020-2021. The thematic areas of interest include social media marketing, influencer marketing, and consumer engagement, and emerging areas of interest, including TikTok, artificial intelligence, and data-driven analytics, reflect the changes in technology. The findings highlight the interdisciplinary and international expanding nature of viral marketing studies. The analysis defines the intellectual architecture and recent development of theme, making the study a good contribution to the discipline.

detail.title: Understanding Perceptions of Metaverse Personalization Technologies Among Early-Career Professionals
detail.abstract: ​​ This study investigates which factors influence early-career professionals' willingness to advocate for personalization technologies in the Metaverse. Personalizing consumer experience has become a strategic element for companies seeking to increase customer satisfaction and revenue. As the Metaverse gains traction, supported by virtual reality (VR), augmented reality (AR), blockchain, and artificial intelligence (AI), understanding emerging professionals' perceptions becomes increasingly relevant for organizations planning digital transformation strategies. A quantitative empirical study was conducted using an online questionnaire distributed to a convenience sample of 100 early-career professionals. Data were analysed through Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM) using SmartPLS 4. The conceptual model, grounded in the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT), examines five latent constructs, perceived advantages, perceived benefits, resources and human capital, perceived risks, and trust, and their influence on willingness to advocate. Perceived advantages (β = 0.459, p < 0.001) and perceived benefits (β = 0.445, p < 0.001) are the primary drivers of advocacy willingness. Organizational resources exert a significant indirect effect mediated by perceived benefits (β = 0.152, p = 0.008). Contrary to established trust-risk theory, trust positively influenced risk perception (β = 0.732, p < 0.001), suggesting familiarity with Metaverse technologies heightens rather than diminishes risk awareness. Neither perceived risks nor trust demonstrated a significant direct effect on willingness_to advocate. These findings extend trust–risk–value frameworks to immersive Metaverse contexts, offering insights into early-career professionals' advocacy readiness and practical implications for organisations promoting Metaverse personalization strategies.

detail.abstract: How do citizens evaluate government economic performance? Although both economic perceptions and partisan identity are known to shape political attitudes, their interaction remains poorly understood. This study develops a Partisan Disconfirmation Model (PDM), integrating expectancy-disconfirmation theory (EDT) with partisan identity to explain how citizens form satisfaction judgments about government economic management. The study uses a nationally representative Afrobarometer survey data from Malawi (N = 1,200). Ordered logistic regression models are estimated to examine how perceptions of national economic conditions and partisan identification influence satisfaction with government economic management. The analysis includes interaction terms to assess whether partisan effects vary across economic contexts. Hypotheses are evaluated using omnibus Wald tests of joint parameter significance, alongside post-estimation contrasts based on predicted probabilities. Perceived economic performance emerges as the strongest predictor of satisfaction, with more positive evaluations significantly increasing the likelihood of favourable assessments of government economic management. Partisan alignment also shapes evaluations, as ruling-party identifiers report higher satisfaction than opposition supporters. While joint tests confirm the independent effects of economic perceptions and partisanship, post-estimation contrasts provide no evidence that partisan effects vary across economic contexts, indicating that these influences operate independently rather than conditionally. The findings highlight the central role of economic performance perceptions in shaping satisfaction with government economic management. Although partisanship influences baseline attitudes, the absence of conditional partisan belief updating suggests that economic perceptions and partisan identity exert independent effects, rather than interacting through a disconfirmation process as predicted by the PDM.

title: Digital Capacity and Labor Productivity in Europe: Evidence from Threshold and Dynamic Panel Models
affiliations: Istanbul Aydin University, Istanbul Aydin University and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Digital Capacity and Labor Productivity in Europe: Evidence from Threshold and Dynamic Panel Models
detail.abstract: This study examines the impact of digitalization on labor productivity across 27 European countries from 2014 to 2023. Using panel data methods with country and year fixed effects, the analysis explores whether digital capacity, measured by internet usage, improves productivity and if this effect differs across various levels of human capital. The results show that internet usage has a positive and statistically significant impact on labor productivity. This finding remains consistent across various models, including dynamic ones that incorporate lagged internet usage. Contrary to usual expectations, the analysis does not indicate significant nonlinear or threshold effects based on human capital. A formal difference test confirms that the effect of digitalization does not vary significantly between low and high human capital regimes. Additional robustness checks indicate that alternative measures of digitalization, such as cloud computing adoption, do not show a significant relationship with productivity. This implies that basic digital infrastructure, rather than more advanced digital technologies, plays a more crucial role in boosting productivity. Overall, the findings emphasize the wide and inclusive scope of digitalization, showing that its benefits are not limited to high-skill economies. From a policy standpoint, the results highlight the importance of increasing internet access as a key factor in boosting economic performance and long-term productivity growth.

detail.abstract: We develop a theoretical framework in which artificial intelligence produces economic output through sequential search rather than one-shot mapping. When task completion requires iterative generation, evaluation, and revision, the economically relevant quantity is tokens per completed task, not tokens per response. We show that nominal deflation in the unit price of compute and inflation in the token intensity of completed tasks can coexist-an indexnumber problem analogous to the gap between nominal and real price indices. The central constraint we identify is not on the marginal frontier task but on the aggregate compute required to substitute AI for cognitive labor at scale: under sequential-search production with convex token demand in task complexity, the integral of token requirements over a broad task distribution grows faster than capacity can plausibly expand unless within-task efficiency improves rapidly enough to outpace endogenous complexity growth. We formalize this as a race between two rates, characterize the conditions under which broad substitution is feasible, and derive a set of testable implications for the distribution of compute across tasks, the structure of pricing, and the pattern of occupational exposure.

title: GLP-1 Use as a Distributed Decision System
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: GLP-1 Use as a Distributed Decision System
detail.abstract:
Recent GLP-1 use beyond narrow formal indications can be read not only as a medical phenomenon but as a distributed decision system characterized by local signal generation, user-side interpretation, strong execution at the level of the individual user, and weak institutional observability. This paper treats that domain as a sharp case-extension for structural observability in AI-augmented decision architectures rather than as a substitute theory of digital health. The analytical focus is not therapeutic efficacy as such, but the architecture through which physiological and behavioral signals are produced, transformed, thresholded, and acted upon across partially connected actors.

The paper builds on the signal-execution distinction and a broader emerging observability stack that includes Control Signal Mapping, the Accountability-Influence Metric, the Override Density Index, the Signal Attenuation Index, and Decision Engagement Rate. The revision sharpens the clinical-informatics boundary: the relevant object is not only AI advice, and not only generative AI, but the signal-to-action pathway through which computer-generated recommendations, patient-generated signals, peer interpretation, prescribing interfaces, and user-side digital interpretation become review, action, override, delay, or non-action.

The contribution is conceptual and architectural, not clinical. The paper argues that contemporary GLP-1 use is best treated as a concentrated contemporary instance of distributed experimentation with strong local execution and weak reconstructability. It adds one operational layer of sharpness by making the domain topology explicit, translating the metric stack directly into the case, connecting the case to clinical decision-support workflow integration, and outlining a later empirical trace and calibration design without prematurely closing the framework.

Status of this draft. This version is prepared as a replacement SSRN preprint. It is positioned as a sharp application and case-extension paper, not as a paper that replaces the main theoretical line on structural observability in AI-supported decision architectures and not as the first full publication of the metric stack. It is also not clinical guidance. The theoretical spine is fixed elsewhere: signal versus execution, structural observability, corrective reachability, and the broader observability framework. What remains intentionally compact here is the domain translation: how that spine behaves when the decision environment is a large, user-controlled, partially networked health experimentation field with incomplete institutional visibility.

title: An Enterprise AI Governance Maturity Model for Cloud-deployed Generative AI Systems

detail.title: An Enterprise AI Governance Maturity Model for Cloud-deployed Generative AI Systems
detail.abstract: Scalable cloud services, built-in security tooling, and accelerating competition are the factors behind the rapid enterprise integration of Generative AI into Microsoft Azure ecosystems (Ettinger; Biswas). Organizations are starting to use Azure-native GenAI to make their operations more productive, improve analytics, and engage with customers, and address emerging governance and risk management challenges (Biswas; Schiros et al.). It is a case of the creation of a systematic AI governance maturity model with a specific focus on Azure-based Generative AI implementations (Wairagade and Govindarajan; Rangan and Yoost). It was intended to have the enterprise goals to match the patterns of the Azure architecture, platform services, and realities of operations in various organizational settings (Rangan and Yoost; Ettinger). The methodology is a literature review and synthesis of enterprise architecture literature, developed governance frameworks, and operational practice of cloud GenAI (Denni-Fiberesima; Marchena Sekli and De La Vega). Integration of strategic, technical and organizational perspectives was done through comparative analysis to create a coherent and action-oriented maturity structure (Denni-Fiberesima; Wairagade and Govindarajan). The most important observations show that there are six dimensions of core governance capabilities, namely: strategy, architecture, security, compliance, operations and value realization (MODEL, 2024; Kongsten and Kathirgamadas). These dimensions indicate common enterprise pain points in large scale Azure GenAI deployments and regulatory landscapes (Kongsten and Kathirgamadas; Biswas). The maturity model categorizes capabilities into stages of progression supporting the controlled experimentation, standardized deployment, and optimization on an enterprise-wide level (MODEL, 2024; Rangan and Yoost). The main finding is that a progressive model of governance maturity makes it possible to adopt Generative AI in an Azure environment in a scaled, secure, and responsible way (Biswas; Schiros et al.).

title: Analysis of the Factors Influencing the Performance of Listed Commercial Banks in China

detail.title: Analysis of the Factors Influencing the Performance of Listed Commercial Banks in China
detail.abstract: This article examines the determinants of performance among Chinese commercial banks listed on the A-share market from 2011 to 2019. The study responds to two persistent issues in the bankingperformance literature. First, profitability alone does not fully capture bank performance because commercial banks are highly leveraged financial intermediaries whose social and regulatory function depends on solvency, liquidity and asset-quality management. Second, listed rural commercial banks differ from state-owned, joint-stock and city commercial banks in ownership history, customer base, geographic embeddedness and credit-risk exposure, but the empirical meaning of this distinction must be theoretically justified rather than assumed. Using panel data for 32 listed commercial banks, the article measures profitability through return on assets (ROA) and risk-management capability through the non-performing loan (NPL) ratio. The explanatory variables include capital adequacy, provision coverage, liquidity, leverage, bank size, GDP, money supply, real-estate activity and stock-market turnover. The findings suggest that provision coverage, loan-to-deposit ratios, leverage and size are important internal determinants of performance, while macroeconomic and market variables affect asset quality differently across rural and non-rural banks. The results further indicate that the bankperformance effects of scale, liquidity and credit-risk buffers are heterogeneous: rural commercial banks are more exposed to local credit-market structure and balance-sheet constraints, whereas nonrural banks are more responsive to macro-financial conditions. The article contributes by integrating the bank profitability, risk-management and institutional heterogeneity literatures, by explicitly addressing endogeneity and model-design limitations, and by providing policy implications for bank regulation, asset-quality supervision and high-quality financial development in China.

title: Coordination Failures and Stackelberg Leadership in Housing Development with Network Effects
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Coordination Failures and Stackelberg Leadership in Housing Development with Network Effects
detail.abstract: I study coordination failures in housing development markets with network effects, where the value of building depends on aggregate supply. When network effects are sufficiently strong and convex, multiple equilibria arise: a low-supply coordination failure and a high-supply outcome. Without a coordination mechanism, equilibrium is indeterminate. I introduce a large developer who moves first in a Stackelberg game, committing to housing supply before atomistic developers make entry decisions. The main result is that the large developer always commits at least to the high-supply equilibrium, eliminating the coordination failure by pushing past the unstable threshold that separates the low and high outcomes. The result is unconditional; it holds for general demand functions and cost distributions, and does not depend on which stable continuation equilibrium materializes. The leader’s commitment inverts standard monopoly intuition: first-mover commitment can improve welfare by resolving a coordination problem that atomistic markets cannot solve on their own. I also characterize when the developer builds beyond the high equilibrium into a monopoly region, and show that the market underprovides housing relative to the social optimum.

detail.abstract: The conflict in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is a complex system of multidimensional interactions involving Congolese institutional fragility, endogenous community dynamics, transnational war economies and structural regional interference. This analysis takes a Congolese perspective that deciphers the mechanisms of conflict reproduction without adhering to exogenous narratives that legitimise regional aggression. Beyond the simplistic dichotomy between “Tutsi” and “non-Tutsi” groups, the mappi ng of armed actors reveals differentiated trajectories of community militarisation, fragmented state capture and increasing hybridisation of belligerent motivations. The two Congo wars (1996–2003) and the ongoing conflict remain structured by hybrid logics combining regional invasion, the recomposition of national political power, and roots in local territorial dynamics. A sustainable policy of prevention and reparation requires the coherent integration of five pillars: land reform, early warning systems, d ismantling of the war economy, professionalised security governance, and verifiable regional diplomacy.

detail.title: End-to-End Head-Tracking Virtual Sensing Using a Temporal Convolutional Network for Active Road Noise Control
detail.abstract: Head-tracking active road noise control requires accurate virtual sensing of sound pressure at the occupants’ ear. Conventional approaches based on the remote microphone method (RMM) remain limited because the use of one observation filter per head position does not account for dynamic driving conditions and provides insufficient information for robust model training. This study proposed an end-to-end head-tracking virtual sensing framework that uses a temporal convolutional network conditioned on the head-position information via feature-wise linear modulation. The proposed model predicts time-domain virtual microphone signals from eight-channel physical microphone measurements and real-time head positions. This formulation enables the segmentation of long recordings into numerous overlapping input–output pairs, thereby providing richerㅇ supervision and enabling the model to capture variations in road noise characteristics across different operating conditions. Experimental results indicated that the proposed method significantly outperformed the conventional RMM-based approach, reducing the virtual sensing error from -14.79 to -19.05 dB in NMSE and from -11.52 to -17.07 dBA in A-weighted spectral error. Moreover, the measurement time per head-pose condition could be reduced without a considerable loss in accuracy when sufficient variability in operating conditions was preserved. Furthermore, the encoder–decoder structure effectively reduced the computational cost while maintaining comparable frequency-domain performance within the control band. Active noise control (ANC) simulations demonstrated that the improved virtual sensing accuracy resulted in enhanced control performance, and the proposed method achieved ANC results close to those obtained using actual measured signals without virtual sensing, indicating near-optimal performance.

title: The joke goes like this: A physicist, an engineer and an economist are stranded in the desert…

detail.title: The joke goes like this: A physicist, an engineer and an economist are stranded in the desert…
detail.abstract: A joke about economists "assuming a can opener" sarcastically exposes mainstream economics' tendency to abstract away from real social conditions, replacing lived complexity with tidy theoretical models. Economic sociology challenges this detachment by foregrounding power, inequality, institutions, and culture, insisting that economic behavior must be understood as it unfolds in the real world rather than within frictionless and therefore essentially erroneous models in economics.

detail.abstract: External pressure does not produce uniform political outcomes. This article explains why sanctions and coercive strategies that contributed to fragmentation in Venezuela instead reinforced institutional cohesion in Iran. Drawing on comparative institutional analysis, it argues that the effectiveness of external pressure depends not on its intensity but on the structure of the target state. In fragmented systems, pressure accelerates disarticulation; in cohesive systems with integrated elite networks, it can consolidate authority. Iran’s dual security architecture, quasi-state economic networks, and geopolitical positioning enable it to absorb and redirect external shocks. By contrast, Venezuela’s fragmented institutional structure amplified the destabilizing effects of sanctions. The article concludes that effective policy requires structural diagnosis and targeted pressure rather than broad coercive strategies that risk reinforcing regime resilience.

detail.title: Hedge Fund Awards: Do Investors and Managers Care, and Should They?
detail.abstract: Using a global sample of hedge fund awards (HFAs), we document that award winners and nominees attract significant investor flows without exhibiting subsequent outperformance. These results suggest that HFAs function effectively as marketing tools, while raising questions about the sophistication of capital allocation in the hedge fund industry. Crucially, we uncover a novel, within-year pattern of return manipulation: award-eligible top performers engage in significantly more return smoothing in the second half of the year compared to non-eligible peers. This strategic smoothing is distinct from midyear risk-shifting and points to potential distortions in the return data reported by eligible funds, particularly after strong year-to-date returns.

title: Event Contracts as "Primitive" Securities

detail.title: Event Contracts as "Primitive" Securities
detail.abstract:
Some types of event contracts are not derivatives.  They belong to a special class of instruments known as Arrow-Debreu or “primitive” securities in financial economics.  Many of the most politically salient event contracts¬—such as election, political, “mention” and “culture” contracts—fit this category of instruments.  These sui generis instruments are not contingent claims based on the price of an asset or the level of an index; rather, they are contingent claims based on the affirmative act or failure to act of an underlying entity.  As such, they raise novel issues unaddressed by federal derivatives regulation.  First, the subjects of these contracts—an election candidate, a public official, a corporate executive, a performer, etc.—may have agency over their outcomes; that is, the underlying entity may control the resolution.  Second, the outcome of these contracts may be ambiguous; that is, the resolution may be only subjectively determined.  

Because primitive securities are so different from derivatives, they should not be regulated as such.  This paper develops a taxonomy of event contracts and proposes a disclosure-based scheme of regulation for those that qualify as primitive securities.  The scheme has several elements, all intended to promote the integrity and accuracy of prediction markets, and is informed both by securities markets regulation and federal campaign finance regulation.  First, it empowers federal regulators—presumably, the CFTC, but possibly the SEC—with the authority to declare which event contracts must be regulated as primitive securities.  Second, it requires Designated Contract Markets (DCMs) to disclose all contractual arrangements with prediction market investors, including but not limited to liquidity providers, and the subjects of event contracts.  Third, it requires DCMs to disclose their resolution mechanisms and the deliberations of the resolution mechanism for each outcome resolved.  Finally—and most controversially—it requires DCMs to disclose the identity and position of all investors in primitive securities shortly after the time of trade.

title: An Isomorphic non-Rotemberg Flexible-Price Model for the New Keynesian Model
affiliations: University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign

detail.title: An Isomorphic non-Rotemberg Flexible-Price Model for the New Keynesian Model
detail.abstract: It is shown that if a flexible-price model is generalized to include an inflation wedge in the aggregate production function, it becomes isomorphic to the New Keynesian model without requiring separate inflation-related adjustment costs or sticky prices. This formulation does not require finitely many firms, though an intermediate goods sector with monopolistic competition is utilized for aggregation. Potential problems with the functional form of the inflation wedge are examined. A comparison against the Rotemberg adjustment cost model is provided, highlighting the distinction between unused but wasted resources (Rotemberg) and production efficiency (our model). The paradox of flexibility in a New Keynesian model under the zero lower bound is reexamined in light of this alternative flexible-price framework.

Using data from the World Bank Enterprise Surveys covering over 45,000 firms across 50 developing countries from 2006 to 2019, this study investigates whether financial openness reduces the dispersion of total factor productivity across firms within industries.

title: Shortfall Aversion On A Finite Horizon
affiliations: University of Dayton

detail.title: Shortfall Aversion On A Finite Horizon
detail.abstract: This paper solves an optimal consumption-investment problem for an investor with shortfall aversion and risk aversion on a finite horizon in closed form solution. The investor's optimal solution is to adjust the spending rate and portfolio weight based on the ratio of wealth to historical maximal consumption. Compared to those in traditional models, the spending rate is more stable. Moreover, the portfolio weight decreases when time is closer to horizon; this is consistent with the allocation strategy that typically suggested by financial advisors.

detail.abstract: Using 18 months of hourly data on Hyperliquid and Binance perpetual contracts for BTC, ETH, SOL, DOGE, and AVAX, I show that the perpetual-spot basis predicts Binance perpetual realized volatility. In the pooled cross-coin specification with structural break controls, the absolute basis significantly predicts forward volatility at all three horizons (h = 1, 8, 24; t = 2.04, 4.44, 4.72). Percoin estimates show BTC's coefficient is essentially zero, consistent with limits-to-arbitrage frictions absent at the most-liquid coin; the four other coins all show positive coefficients, with individual significance for SOL and DOGE. Out-of-sample testing produces statistically significant forecast improvements against a simple lagged-volatility benchmark but not against the more demanding HAR-RV benchmark.

detail.abstract: This paper diagnoses the crisis of capitalist social reproduction as a structural failure of market mechanisms and the bureaucratic state, conceptualised as 'Dispositional Alienation'. Drawing on Cambridge social ontology and the Sraffian surplus approach, we propose a 'Fourth Property Regime' via the Citizen's Executive Right (CER). The CER unbundles fiscal property, transferring surplus disposition to citizens via Personal Public Accounts. To circumvent liquidity preference and sovereign lag, the system embeds algorithmic demurrage inspired by Gesellian stamped money. Through Stock-Flow Consistent accounting and non-linear dynamics, we demonstrate that this temporal friction acts as a macroeconomic viscous damper. By forcing zero-deficit mobilisation into non-commodified Civic Syndicates, the protocol unwinds the Goodwin limit cycle. The CER provides a cybernetic infrastructure that subordinates the surplus to democratic social reproduction, immunising the public sphere against volatility and financialisation. This offers a structural foundation for an economics of sufficiency.

title: A Decomposition of Relational Utility: Status and Achievement

detail.title: A Decomposition of Relational Utility: Status and Achievement

keywords: wealth and well-being JEL Codes: D60

detail.abstract: This paper proposes a decomposition of relational utility into two distinct components:Status Utility and Achievement Utility. While existing approaches treat comparison-based utility as a single mechanism, the analysis developed here shows that evaluative well-being arises through both externally anchored and internally anchored processes. Status Utility reflects the value placed on relative position within a reference group, whereas Achievement Utility reflects the value placed on progress relative to personal benchmarks, including past performance, goals, and aspirations. A central implication of this decomposition is that relational utility is characterized by the coexistence of multiple evaluative mechanisms rather than by a single, shifting process. Unlike experiential utility, which tends to exhibit systematic changes in composition across the wealth distribution, status-based and achievement-based evaluations may operate simultaneously at all levels of wealth. The relative importance of these components varies across individuals, reflecting heterogeneity in evaluative orientation. By distinguishing between status and achievements components, the framework developed in this paper provides a mechanism-based interpretation of how wealth generates comparison-based utility. The analysis clarifies that changes in well-being depend not only on wealth itself, but also on how outcomes are evaluated-whether in terms of relative position or personal progress. These results complement existing work on the decomposition of total utility and establish a foundation for further analysis of marginal utility and empirical patterns of well-being.

title: From Concept to On-Chain An Institutional Playbook for Tokenization Structuring, Governance, and Lifecycle Management

detail.title: From Concept to On-Chain An Institutional Playbook for Tokenization Structuring, Governance, and Lifecycle Management
detail.abstract: This paper examines the tokenization of real-world assets (RWAs) through an institutional lens, arguing that the primary constraints on adoption are structural rather than technological. While distributed ledger technology (DLT) has made it feasible to represent ownership, transfer value, and automate execution on-chain, institutional viability is determined by legal enforceability, governance design, lifecycle management, and integration with existing financial systems. The analysis is organized as a lifecycle playbook, covering asset selection, legal structuring, governance design, issuance, servicing, and secondary market behavior. Across each stage, the paper identifies recurring failure modes that prevent tokenization initiatives from moving beyond pilot environments, including weak legal anchoring, undefined authority structures, insufficient servicing infrastructure, and misaligned liquidity assumptions. Drawing on examples from tokenized funds, private credit, and infrastructure, as well as regulatory developments in Singapore, United States, Hong Kong, and Abu Dhabi, the paper shows that institutional adoption is converging toward models that embed tokenization within existing legal and regulatory frameworks rather than replacing them. The central conclusion is that tokenization should be understood not as a technological innovation, but as an extension of financial market infrastructure. Systems that prioritize governance, enforceability, and lifecycle management are more likely to achieve institutional scale, while those that focus primarily on on-chain execution remain confined to experimental use cases.

title: Gendered e-commerce adoption among rural Indonesian entrepreneurs: Determinants and income impact (corrected version)

detail.title: Gendered e-commerce adoption among rural Indonesian entrepreneurs: Determinants and income impact (corrected version)

contentType.other: Corrected version of the published one

detail.abstract: This study examines the gendered determinants of e-commerce adoption among rural entrepreneurs in Indonesia and evaluates its impact on income, addressing the gap in ruraland gender-disaggregated evidence in the digital economy literature. Using nationally representative Sakernas data (2018-2024), this study employs probit models to estimate adoption determinants and applies gender-disaggregated income regressions, Propensity Score Matching, and quantile regression to assess causal and heterogeneous incom e effects. Education and training significantly increase adoption, while age, marital status, and household constraints, particularly for women, reduce participation. E-commerce adoption raises income substantially, with male entrepreneurs gaining higher returns (around 30.8 percent) than female entrepreneurs (17.5 percent). Quantile results show stronger equalizing effects among lower-income men, while gains for women are smaller and more evenly distributed. The findings highlight the need for gender-sensitive digital inclusion policies that go beyond infrastructure to address capability gaps, time constraints, and structural barriers limiting women's participation and returns in the digital economy. This study contributes by integrating gender and rural perspectives using nationally representative data and robust causal methods, offering new evidence on heterogeneous income effects of digital adoption in developing economies.

title: ASSESSING ROOF WIND LOADS ON LOW-RISE BUILDINGS UNDER GUST-FRONT-LIKE FLOWS USING ABL WIND TUNNEL SIMULATION
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Concordia University

detail.title: ASSESSING ROOF WIND LOADS ON LOW-RISE BUILDINGS UNDER GUST-FRONT-LIKE FLOWS USING ABL WIND TUNNEL SIMULATION
detail.abstract: This study addresses a critical gap in the current understanding of downburst-induced wind loads on low-rise buildings, a topic that remains underrepresented in existing literature despite its importance for residential and industrial structures. An experimental investigation was conducted to assess the roof wind loads generated by a steady-state gust-front-like flow developed in conventional Atmospheric Boundary Layer (ABL) Wind Tunnel. Two building models, fully immersed in the high velocity approaching outflow, with identical plan dimensions (60 m × 60 m) and differing heights (10 m and 20 m), were tested at a 1:400 scale under seven approach wind directions. The study examines the influence of building height and orientation on the distribution and magnitude of wind-induced pressures. Additionally, the roof pressure coefficients are evaluated against the design provisions of ASCE/SEI 7 for synoptic wind events. The findings highlight that the current provisions are generally adequate for evaluating the effects of gust-front winds on low-rise buildings, while also emphasizing the importance of continued investigations to support future research and codification efforts.

title: Cost-Effectiveness of Aerial Mitigation Strategies for Rapid Wildfire Suppression in California
affiliations: Columbia University, Columbia University, Columbia University,  and Columbia University

detail.title: Cost-Effectiveness of Aerial Mitigation Strategies for Rapid Wildfire Suppression in California
detail.abstract: Wildfire events in California are escalating causing catastrophic economic, ecological, and health losses. Existing wildfire suppression methods are under strain, and traditional insurance-based recovery models are becoming inadequate as insurers withdraw from high-risk markets. This study evaluates the economic efficiency of investing in a state-wide aerial technology solution for rapid wildfire suppression in California from the perspective of insurance companies. The solution combines a network of fire-detection drones surveying all vegetated land in California continuously throughout the year, along with state-owned Super Scooper planes on stand-by for fire-suppression. While nature-based solutions can help build long term resilience, aerial technology is an effective short-term approach to curb increasing damages. A comprehensive cost-benefit analysis reveals a highly favorable Benefit Cost Ratio of 134, indicating that for every dollar invested insurers could realize $134 savings in avoided claim payouts due to wildfires. In other words, the proposed solution would need to prevent less than 1% of expected future wildfire-related insured damages to reach its break-even point, a threshold robust across various sensitivity analyses. The result remained robust across various sensitivity analyses, and this report further discusses why this could be a conservative estimate. The findings of this study strongly support investment in proactive aerial technologies for rapid wildfire mitigation in the face of growing disasters, while nature-based forest management solutions pick pace.

title: Severe Multi-Operator Mobile Network Disruption during the 2025 Southern Thailand Floods: A Swiss Cheese Model Analysis of Telecommunications Resilience
affiliations: Thammasat University

detail.title: Severe Multi-Operator Mobile Network Disruption during the 2025 Southern Thailand Floods: A Swiss Cheese Model Analysis of Telecommunications Resilience
detail.abstract: Severe telecommunications disruption during floods can constrain help requests, emergency coordination, public information, and operational visibility at the same time that response needs intensify. This study analyzes the 2025 Southern Thailand flood telecommunications disruption through the Swiss Cheese Model to explain how infrastructure dependencies and protective layers interacted during breakdown and restoration. The article uses a qualitative-dominant single-case study design with descriptive quantitative support from a sanitized analytical extract prepared from a private operational coordination logbook maintained contemporaneously by the author. The extract combines chronological response records with daily anonymized mobile-network outage counts. In the recorded operational dataset, site-down counts rose from 335 on 2025-11-23 to a peak of 940 on 2025-11-26, then declined to the first all-zero row on 2025-12-06. These counts are reported as recorded site-down counts in the operational dataset and are not interpreted as population coverage, customer-level impact, or complete loss of service everywhere. The findings indicate severe multi-operator telecommunications disruption shaped by flood exposure, electrical power dependency, mobilesite vulnerability, field-access constraints, backup power and fuel logistics, emergency communication workarounds, data-platform interoperability, and institutional coordination. The study contributes by extending Swiss Cheese Model analysis to disaster telecommunications resilience and by showing why layered emergency communications should be treated as a core disaster risk reduction capacity in flood-prone regions.

title: Do Meritocratic Evaluations Encourage Women to Enter Male-Majority Workplaces? Experimental Evidence
affiliations: University of Utah, Max Planck Institute for Innovation and Competition and

detail.title: Do Meritocratic Evaluations Encourage Women to Enter Male-Majority Workplaces? Experimental Evidence
detail.abstract: We study whether anticipated discrimination affect workers’ preferences for entering a competitive hiring process in an online experiment. Our experimental design exogenously varies whether i) the hiring process is meritocratic—the best performing worker in a pair is always hired—or subjective—based on a manager’s evaluation, and ii) the gender of the other worker and manager. Our primary focus is on female workers in male-majority environments, where anticipated discrimination may be particularly salient. Contrary to our hypothesis, we find no significant effect of meritocratic versus subjective evaluation on women’s willingness to enter the hiring process. Heterogeneity analyses provide suggestive evidence that women who believe they are the best performers exhibit a stronger preference for meritocratic evaluations. However, the estimated effect size is moderate and does not vary with the gender composition of other workers.

title: Integrated HAZOP, LOPA, and Markov Model for Safety Integrity Level Assessment: A Case Study of a Hydrogenation Unit
affiliations: China University of Petroleum (East China), China University of Petroleum (East China), Hohai University, China University of Petroleum (East China) and China University of Petroleum (East China)

detail.title: Integrated HAZOP, LOPA, and Markov Model for Safety Integrity Level Assessment: A Case Study of a Hydrogenation Unit
detail.abstract: With the increasing adoption of functional safety standards for Safety Instrumented Systems (SIS)—which serve as a critical independent protection layer in petrochemical operations—the assessment of Safety Integrity Level (SIL) has become a primary focus of industrial safety management. This study investigates a kerosene hydrogenation unit within a petroleum refining enterprise, employing a robust integrated framework of qualitative and quantitative methodologies to evaluate SIS performance. The research methodology follows a systematic three-stage approach, beginning with a Hazard and Operability (HAZOP) analysis to identify critical hazard scenarios requiring rigorous quantitative scrutiny. Subsequently, a Layer of Protection Analysis (LOPA) is applied as a semi-quantitative technique to allocate safety requirements and determine the target SIL for specific safety instrumented interlock loops. Finally, a Markov model is utilized to verify the achieved SIL of these interlock loops against the defined safety requirements. Based on the integrated "HAZOP-LOPA" analysis and the subsequent Markov verification, this paper proposes targeted technical enhancements for the kerosene hydrogenation unit’s SIS, providing a systematic reference for the safety integrity assessment and optimization of comparable petrochemical processing units.

title: Payments in Transition: Technology, Incentives, and the Rise of Digital Infrastructure

detail.title: Payments in Transition: Technology, Incentives, and the Rise of Digital Infrastructure
detail.abstract:
This paper examines the structural evolution of payments systems, focusing on the transition from fragmented, intermediary-driven models toward more integrated, data-enabled digital ecosystems. Historically shaped by regulatory constraints, domestic market structures, and incumbent-controlled networks, payments systems have exhibited persistent inefficiencies, opacity, limited interoperability, and misaligned incentives — not as market failures, but as features of systems designed to extract rather than create value.

A set of macro trends — advances in APIs and open banking, accelerating mobile adoption, generational behavioral shifts, and maturing regulatory frameworks — is compressing the timeline for structural change. New entrants and platform companies are redefining the competitive landscape by embedding payments within broader digital ecosystems, leveraging user data to expand into adjacent financial services, and systematically unbundling functions that incumbents have historically bundled for margin.

Incumbent institutions are responding through infrastructure modernization, strategic partnerships, and selective investment, but remain constrained by legacy architectures and revenue models that depend on the inefficiencies they are being asked to eliminate. The result is a competitive environment where the decisive battleground is shifting from transaction processing toward control of interfaces, data, and settlement infrastructure.

The paper argues that payments are evolving from a standalone financial service into foundational digital infrastructure — a layer upon which broader economic activity will increasingly depend. Early developments in distributed ledger technologies, digital assets, and programmable transaction frameworks point toward a further structural shift in how settlement, interoperability, and compliance are designed and governed. These developments remain nascent as of 2019, but their trajectory — shaped by the convergence of forces this paper describes — points toward a more fundamental redesign of payments infrastructure than the industry has yet fully absorbed.

The analysis has direct implications for financial institutions evaluating digital strategy, platform companies expanding into financial services, and policymakers and regulators designing frameworks for an ecosystem in transition.

title: The Role of Commercial Actors in Cislunar Regime Formation
affiliations: Georgia Institute of Technology

detail.title: The Role of Commercial Actors in Cislunar Regime Formation
detail.abstract: Activity on and around the Moon has increased significantly in recent years, with participation from a wide array of countries and private actors. Activity is expected to continue to grow, resulting in important geopolitical, economic, and security implications. Amidst this growth, there is concern that the current governance regime is insufficient to deal with emerging challenges. Regime development is particularly difficult in multi-stakeholder environments where values and interests may differ significantly. This paper focuses on the role of the private sector in governance development. Through semi-structured interviews with 19 private sector cislunar actors, this paper identifies common concerns and perspectives within this group, including an emphasis limiting regime development in order to allow experimentation and failure in the early phases of Lunar development. These interviews suggest that a limited, flexible regime focused primarily on coordination, information sharing, and avoiding irreversible damage to the Lunar environment is seen as most likely to support sustainable growth of Lunar activity.

title: VPNet: A New Explainable-AI Paradigm for Tractable Multimodal,Multidimensional Classification with Probabilistic Circuits on ViT Features

detail.title: VPNet: A New Explainable-AI Paradigm for Tractable Multimodal,Multidimensional Classification with Probabilistic Circuits on ViT Features
detail.abstract: Deep learning-based classification models can understand and extract complex representations or relationships between classes. If the decision process of such AI can be visualized in a way that humans can understand, this may create the potential for AI tools to assist in new scientific discoveries or for more trustworthy AI models. However, such visualizations produced by current XAI methods, including Grad-CAM and attention maps, are theoretically questionable.To overcome this limitation, we propose a novel theoretically explainable AI model for classification tasks that can handle multimodal and multidimensional information. Unlike traditional classification models based on convolutional neural networks or transformers, our approach combines probabilistic circuits with two vision transformers, DINO and CLIP, enabling probabilistic interpretability at the patch level, encoder level, and modality level. We demonstrate that our proposed method can overcome the randomized test for saliency checks, a test that current state-of-the-art XAI models often fail. Additionally, this study shows the explainability of the model's decisions at the patch, encoder, and modality levels, while achieving strong generalization performance across various classification tasks.

detail.abstract: The institutions of rule of law have become a key factor for inclusive economic development, but the main strands of the literature involve theoretically driven expectations. Therefore, the study sought to examine the impact of the institutions of the rule of law on inclusive economic development in the African Union. While extant studies focused on the effect of governance on national output, the present study goes beyond growth by including inequality-adjusted welfare indicators. We constructed a strongly balanced panel dataset from the World Development Indicators, Worldwide Governance Indicators and the United Nations Development Programme for the period from 1990 to 2023, including 54 African countries. The results of the Pool Mean Group-Autoregressive Distributed Lag model reveal that the institutions of the rule of law have a long-run statistically significant relationship with inclusive economic development. The study controlled for trade, investment, official development assistance, labour force, and gross domestic product per capita. The study offers both policy suggestions and direction for future research.

title: A Novel Solving Algorithm for ELM Models in Online Sequential Learning and Federated Learning Scenarios
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and Chinese Academy of Sciences

detail.title: A Novel Solving Algorithm for ELM Models in Online Sequential Learning and Federated Learning Scenarios
detail.abstract: Extreme learning machine (ELM), a type of single-hidden-layer feedforward neural networks (SLFNs), exhibits strong generalization and rapid learning. Enhancing the learning capacity of ELM is crucial for handling large datasets and online learning tasks. To support online sequential learning and federated learning, this paper proposes a novel algorithm for solving ELM Models. First, to tackle the challenges posed by ill-conditioned problems and improve numerical stability, as well as better fit the subsequent solving procedure, a tailored QR factorization is presented in this algorithm. Second, to quickly solve the least-squares problem and avoid computation of the Moore-Penrose generalized inverse, a reduced Greville's method is proposed. Moreover, to facilitate online sequential learning and federated learning, a merging algorithm is introduced for integrating two ELM models. This algorithm adeptly leverages intermediate results from both models, thereby reducing the complexity, and can also seamlessly integrate a regularization term into the model at any time. Utilizing the merging technique, an online sequential learning paradigm and an on-device federated learning framework are enabled. Experiments show the proposed approach offers better performance than existing algorithms.

title: Heterogeneous Ambiguity Aversion and a Novel Cross-Sectional Pricing Factor
affiliations: Ozyegin University - Faculty of Business

detail.title: Heterogeneous Ambiguity Aversion and a Novel Cross-Sectional Pricing Factor
detail.abstract: I derive the cross-sectional asset pricing implications of heterogeneous ambiguity aversion across investors in a multi-asset economy with smooth-ambiguity preferences. The equilibrium pricing equation takes a two-factor form: the excess return on the market portfolio with a CAPMlike ambiguity adjustment, plus a market-orthogonal factor that vanishes under homogeneous aversion or with two uncertain assets. The two channels are governed by distinct moments of the cross-sectional ambiguity-aversion distribution: the first by its risk-tolerance-weighted mean, the second by its variance. Cross-sectional CAPM mispricing should track preference-dispersion proxies, with this effect persisting after controlling for aggregate-uncertainty proxies.
