keywords.keywords: Heterogeneous Federated Learning ；Contract Theory–Driven  ；Adaptive Incentive Mechanism  ；Dynamic Game ；Participation Fairness

detail.abstract: To address information asymmetry, weak behavioral constraints, and performance degradation under client heterogeneity in federated learning, this paper proposes a Contract Theory–Driven Adaptive Incentive Mechanism for Heterogeneous Federated Learning (CTAI-HFL). A multi-dimensional contract menu with base, performance, and loyalty incentives enables type-based self-selection and ensures incentive compatibility while suppressing opportunistic behavior via dynamic game modeling.Under a total budget constraint, a scoring pool normalizes reward allocation, and unit resource efficiency captures the contribution–cost relationship, balancing fairness and resource utilization. A blockchain-enabled architecture combining off-chain computation and on-chain verification ensures verifiability and immutability of incentive execution.Experiments show significant gains in complex heterogeneous environments. Participation disparity across capability groups is reduced from over 14% to within 0.5%. With a normalized total cost of 0.780, the method achieves 89.1% peak accuracy, improving baselines by 7.0%. Moreover, a subjective logic–based reputation mechanism enhances robustness, maintaining about 98% active client retention over 500 rounds and mitigating dropout of low-capability devices.

title: DyG-STEF: A Structural–Temporal Enhanced Transformer for Dynamic Graph Link Prediction
affiliations: Dalian Minzu University, Dalian Minzu University and Dalian Minzu University

detail.title: DyG-STEF: A Structural–Temporal Enhanced Transformer for Dynamic Graph Link Prediction
detail.abstract: Continuous-time dynamic graph (CTDG) link prediction remains challenging because link formation is jointly affected by evolving topology, heterogeneous temporal dependencies, and noisy interactions. Existing methods mainly learn node-level temporal representations, which may encode candidate-edge structural evidence only implicitly and weaken discrimination under inductive or hard-negative settings. This paper proposes DyG-STEF, a structural–temporal enhanced Transformer for CTDG link prediction. DyG-STEF explicitly injects topological priors, including local similarity and global centrality, into candidate-edge representations to strengthen edge-level discrimination. It further introduces a cross-scale temporal encoding module that combines logarithmic, reciprocal, periodic, and learnable temporal channels to capture long-range attenuation, short-term bursts, recurring patterns, and nonlinear temporal relations. To improve training stability, edge-feature reconstruction, adversarial alignment, and contrastive learning are used as training-stage regularizers without adding auxiliary inference branches. Experiments on six real-world datasets under transductive and inductive settings demonstrate that DyG-STEF achieves competitive and often superior performance, especially on frequent-interaction datasets and random negative sampling. Ablation, sensitivity, and perturbation analyses further verify the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed components.

title: Granular growing self-organizing map for novelty detection and incremental feature selection
affiliations: Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications, Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications, Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics and Henan Normal University

detail.title: Granular growing self-organizing map for novelty detection and incremental feature selection
detail.abstract: Incremental feature selection has garnered significant attention in recent years due to its effectiveness in handling dynamically evolving data streams. However, most existing approaches fail to effectively address the dual challenges of label scarcity and novel class emergence in open-world scenarios. Furthermore, the inherent fuzziness in partially labeled data streams can compromise model performance in such scenarios. In this paper, we propose a fusion approach for novelty detection and feature selection in incremental semi-supervised environments. First, a novel granular growing self-organizing map (GGSOM) is constructed by incorporating lower approximations from fuzzy neighborhood granular ball rough sets into neuron initialization and neighborhood construction, enabling effective novelty detection. Second, an incremental update mechanism for fuzzy neighborhood information granules is introduced to allow GGSOM to adaptively optimize its internal representation, thereby assigning more precise cluster labels to incoming unlabeled data. Finally, we develop a GGSOM-based incremental feature selection algorithm (IFS-GGSOM) that dynamically identifies informative features through entropy-based uncertainty measures. Extensive experiments on twelve benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms several state-of-the-art methods in novelty detection and feature selection tasks.

title: Physics-Constrained Dynamic Graph and Multi-Resolution Temporal Modeling for TrafficForecasting
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Physics-Constrained Dynamic Graph and Multi-Resolution Temporal Modeling for TrafficForecasting
detail.abstract: Spatio-temporal traffic forecasting in Intelligent TransportationSystems (ITS) remains challenging due to four persistentinformation-processing limitations: static graph dependenciesthat obscure evolving network topology, insufficient uncertaintyquantification under heterogeneous sensor reliability, uniform temporal resolution that prevents multi-scale information fusion,and physical constraints enforced in isolation without aunified probabilistic learning formulation.In this paper, we propose \textbf{PRISM-ST} (Physics-informedResilient Intelligence for Multi-scale Spatio-TemporalTransportation), a modular framework integrating domain knowledgeencoding with information-theoretic reliability modeling foradaptive prediction from road sensor measurements.PRISM-ST comprises four jointly optimized modules: an Uncertainty-Aware Spectral-Spatial Block (UASSB) forsensor-reliability-weighted spatial embedding via dual-pathwaygraph convolution; a Unified Dynamics and Structure Learning (UDSL) module enforcingtraffic-theoretic constraints through physics-informed neural ODEsand variational structure learning; a Multi-Resolution Temporal Decomposition (MRTD) module enablingvolatility-guided multi-scale information fusion across temporalscales; and an Adaptive Attention-Memory Routing (AAMR) module that provides the horizon-specific prediction head with mixture-of-experts routing. Extensive evaluation on six benchmark datasets ---PeMS03, PeMS04, PeMS07, PeMS08, GBA, and GLA ---demonstrates an average 5.5\% Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) reduction and 2.1\% Mean Absolute Error (MAE) reduction in traffic flow prediction over thestrongest baseline per dataset, spanning competitivegraph-based, Transformer-based, physics-informed, anduncertainty-aware baselines.

title: A Graph-Based Structural Analysis of the Employees' State Insurance Scheme
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: A Graph-Based Structural Analysis of the Employees' State Insurance Scheme
detail.abstract: The Employees' State Insurance (ESI) Scheme constitutes one of India's most extensive social security programmes, providing medical care and income protection to insured persons and their dependants through a complex administrative framework. While prior analyses of ESI data have primarily focused on transactional records such as claims and contributions, relatively limited attention has been paid to the underlying institutional and relational structure that governs benefit eligibility and delivery. This paper presents a graphbased representation of the ESIC administrative system, modelling insured persons, employers, branch offices, and regional offices as interconnected entities. Using administrative datasets with limited transactional coverage, the study demonstrates how graph modelling enables structural analysis, administrative load assessment, and data quality auditing, even in the absence of dense claim data. The findings suggest that graph-based approaches are particularly suited for analysing governance readiness and institutional consistency in large-scale social security systems.

title: The Virtue of Dynamic Factor Loadings for the Chinese Options Market
affiliations: Shanghai University, Shanghai University of Finance and Economics - Shanghai University of Finance and Economics, Students, Shanghai University and Shanghai University

detail.title: The Virtue of Dynamic Factor Loadings for the Chinese Options Market
detail.abstract: Understanding the risk-return trade-off in the options market is difficult with standard observable factor models.  We examine whether dynamic factor loadings improve the explanation of the cross-section of delta-hedged option returns. We apply instrumented principal component analysis (IPCA) to major exchange-traded option products in China. IPCA allows conditional betas to vary with option characteristics, which addresses short contract lifespans and rapidly evolving characteristics. We find that a three-factor IPCA model explains 19.30% of variation in individual option returns and 99.23% in managed portfolios. A bootstrap asset-pricing test fails to reject a zero-alpha restriction. Observable factor models with characteristic-instrumented dynamic betas achieve performance close to IPCA, highlighting the importance of time-varying loadings. We also provide subsample and characteristic-importance analyses.

title: Adapted Beta and the Efficiency of Active Risk: Evidence Across Equity Markets
affiliations: University of Finance and Administration

detail.title: Adapted Beta and the Efficiency of Active Risk: Evidence Across Equity Markets
detail.abstract: This paper examines whether adapted beta, derived from the Minimum Excess Returns Line (MERL) framework, captures a distinct dimension of benchmark-relative risk and whether it has economic relevance for future performance. Using a large cross-market sample of actively managed equity investments across U.S. small cap, international, and emerging markets, we show that adapted beta does not operate as a standalone predictor of excess returns. Instead, its economic role is inherently conditional: adapted beta scales the effectiveness of active risk. In particular, funds combining higher adapted beta with higher tracking error exhibit significantly stronger future risk-adjusted performance and move closer to the benchmark risk–return frontier. This interaction effect is robust across market segments and is most pronounced at medium-term horizons, consistent with the interpretation of adapted beta as a structural measure of active risk efficiency. The findings suggest that the performance of active strategies depends not only on the magnitude of benchmark deviation, but also on the efficiency with which this deviation is transformed into excess returns.

title: Language Experience Reshapes Conceptual Boundaries
affiliations: New York University (NYU) - New York University, New York University (NYU) - New York University, New York University (NYU) - New York University and New York University (NYU) - New York University

detail.title: Language Experience Reshapes Conceptual Boundaries
detail.abstract: Language structures the world into semantic categories that support memory, generalization, and communication. However, semantic categories are not always isomorphic across languages; how bilinguals resolve these cross-linguistic differences remains unclear. This study adopts a controlled, feature-based approach using parametrically manipulated object continua to examine cross-linguistic categorization. English monolinguals, Mandarin monolinguals, and Mandarin-English bilinguals completed a two-alternative forced choice task to test whether bilinguals follow monolingual norms in each language or show an integrated categorization system across languages. While monolingual groups exhibited distinct category boundaries, bilinguals’ categorization did not vary by language—suggesting an integrated categorization system shaped by language exposure. We then trained a neural network model to learn category boundaries under varying language exposure. This model revealed that categorization differences arise from changes in perceptual feature weights. Together, these results suggest that bilinguals’ experiences give rise to a shared conceptual system determined by the combined statistical structure of multiple languages.

title: Closer to New York than to Frankfurt? The Expectations Hypothesis in Poland, the US and the euro area
affiliations: Kozminski University

detail.title: Closer to New York than to Frankfurt? The Expectations Hypothesis in Poland, the US and the euro area
detail.abstract: We re-test the pure expectations hypothesis (peh) on three monthly sovereign zero-coupon curves: a Polish curve tted from quote-driven bondspot venue data, the Gurkaynak Sack Wright Svensson curve for US Treasuries, and the European Central Bank’s Svensson-with-extension t of the euro-area aaa-rated government bond curve. The sample is monthly, 256 observations per market, January 2005 to April 2026. For every market we run the ve classical regression families (Fama Bliss type-1 and type-2, Cochrane Piazzesi two-stage, Thornton conventional and Thornton contrarian) on a horizon-and-maturity grid that mirrors the specication used in the empirical term-structure literature, and draw both asymptotic Newey West hac inference and wild block bootstrap inference. Three modern complements are added: a small-sample Bekaert Hodrick parametric vector autoregression bootstrap, an out-of-sample Diebold Mariano test of the peh-implied forecast against a random-walk benchmark, and a macro-spanning regression that augments Fama Bliss with consumer price in ation, registered unemployment, exchange-rate volatility, and the change in the policy rate. Five ndings stand out. First, the peh cannot be rejected anywhere on the Polish grid under either inference method. Second, asymptotic Newey West inference rejects the peh on the great majority of euro-area horizon-by- maturity pairs, but the wild block bootstrap reduces those rejections by a factor of about twenty. The US sits between, with the handful of asymptotic rejections collapsing to zero under the bootstrap. Third, the Campbell Shiller paradox of wrong-signed contrarian regression coe cients lives on the euroarea sample of this period, not on the Polish or US samples. Fourth, the Cochrane Piazzesi single-factor structure is con rmed in all three markets, with median permaturity loading bn at unity, but joint signi cance of the return-forecasting factor cannot be defended at ve percent under the bootstrap in any of the three markets. Fifth, an auxiliary single-market exhibit on Polish data shows that the forward-spot spread is essentially empty as a predictor (median in-sample R2 at ve percent at any horizon) while a four-element macro vector explains the bulk of the variance of multi-year excess returns and the spread becomes redundant once the macro block is added. We present the macro evidence as a single-market exhibit, with the cross-market generalisation left to a separate companion note. The geography of peh testing on the 2005 2026 sample places Poland closer to New York than to Frankfurt

title: Innovation Strategy Consulting Excellence: The Key Characteristics and The Main Errors

detail.title: Innovation Strategy Consulting Excellence: The Key Characteristics and The Main Errors
detail.abstract: There is growing interest in the global marketplace in innovation. Organizations should always look for innovations so that they can remain competitive. Many CEOs in organizations strongly believe in the power of an effective innovation strategy to better manage their organizational innovation, but by doing so, they feel that they may be usurped. Effective consulting in innovation strategy has four key characteristics and can increase and build rapport with the business environment, inspire employees, and increase their satisfaction with their careers so that they can better become engaged and productive. Strategy consultants can also help client companies avoid four errors in implementing an effective innovation strategy to efficiently deploy organizational capabilities and better manage internal and external sources. The critical findings of this research uncover these key characteristics and solve these main problems for consultants and suggest that to develop an effective innovation strategy, a long-term approach, design thinking, continuous disruptive innovation, and incentive systems improvement must be the organizational mantra.

title: Chenilles légionnaires versus chenilles de karité : Une analyse compensatoire genrée à l'aide d'un nouveau cadre théorique du changement climatique Nom et prénom des auteurs
affiliations: , Thomas Sankara University, Department of Economics, CEDRES and Université Norbert Zongo

detail.title: Chenilles légionnaires versus chenilles de karité : Une analyse compensatoire genrée à l'aide d'un nouveau cadre théorique du changement climatique Nom et prénom des auteurs
detail.abstract: Le changement climatique modifie profondément les dynamiques entomologiques dans les agroécosystèmes sahéliens, entraînant une intensification des attaques de chenilles nuisibles telles que les chenilles légionnaires, tout en perturbant les populations d’espèces entomologiques valorisées comme les chenilles de karité. Cette étude évalue les effets compensatoires entre les pertes agricoles causées par les chenilles légionnaires et les gains issus de l’utilisation des chenilles de karité. Les données d’enquête de terrain réalisées en milieu rural du 10 au 14 février 2025 auprès de 206 ménages agricoles, portant sur les perceptions, les usages entomologiques et les retombées économiques, ont été analysées selon une approche mixte, quantitative et qualitative, pour cerner les logiques locales d’adaptation et les disparités dans la valorisation des ressources naturelles. Les résultats montrent que 81 % des répondants, dont 58 % de femmes, subissent des attaques de chenilles, principalement légionnaires (98 %) et que les gains issus de l’utilisation des chenilles de karité compensent les pertes causées par les chenilles légionnaires que ce soit au niveau de l’échantillon global ou du sous-échantillon genré. En considérant, l’échantillon global, les résultats montrent que les pertes agricoles moyennes s’élèvent à 62 314 FCFA, les gains atteignent 43 694 FCFA et l’impact net moyen est positif à hauteur de 6 690 FCFA. Toutefois, les hommes affichent un impact net négatif (-2 511 FCFA), tandis que les femmes enregistrent un impact net positif (9 627 FCFA). Dans le sous-échantillon des producteurs directement concernés par les pertes et la valorisation des chenilles, l’analyse souligne des disparités genrées. Les pertes moyennes sont de 51 800 FCFA et la compensation moyenne est faible (396 FCFA), avec un excédent de 144 078 FCFA chez les hommes, contre un déficit de -22 778 FCFA chez les femmes. De plus, l’attaque des chenilles légionnaires affectent   le niveau de dépense alimentaire et que la collecte des chenilles de karité affecte positivement le niveau du revenu annuel des ménages. Ces résultats soulignent la nécessité de politiques d’adaptation au changement climatique sensibles aux dynamiques sociales, aux savoirs locaux et à l’inclusion économique des femmes rurales.

title: AI Compass: Measuring Organizational Readiness in the Transition to AI-Native Systems
affiliations: Harvard University, Ashridge Business School - Hult International Business School, Ecole des Ponts ParisTech and Harvard College

detail.title: AI Compass: Measuring Organizational Readiness in the Transition to AI-Native Systems
detail.abstract: This paper introduces AI Compass, a structured diagnostic framework for measuring organizational readiness in the transition from AI-aware to AI-native operational systems. Drawing on the economics of general-purpose technologies, complementary organizational capital, and logistic capability accumulation, we formalize the mechanisms by which AI investment fails to translate into productivity gains in the absence of structural organizational complements. We define organizational AI readiness as a multidimensional vector across five capabilities-AI literacy, data readiness, workflow integration, governance, and strategic alignment-and show that for regulated industries, readiness is governed by a bottleneck specification rather than a weighted average, reflecting the strictly complementary nature of these dimensions. We further derive the social value of readiness measurement as exceeding its private return, grounding the case for treating AI readiness infrastructure as a public good. Empirically, we situate AI Compass within a lineage of measurement frameworks that have preceded comprehensive data collection, and argue that the tool's contextual architecture positions it to generate sector-level comparative data as adoption scales. The paper concludes that accurate readiness measurement is itself a strategic asset, and that organizations which delay structured capability development face a structurally widening gap that cannot be closed by investment alone.

title: Towards a Cyber Resilient Critical Information Infrastructure of India
affiliations: GITAM University, Hyderabad - Kautilya School of Public Policy

detail.title: Towards a Cyber Resilient Critical Information Infrastructure of India
detail.abstract: Cyber ranges are gaining prominence as an operational tool to achieve cyber resilience in an increasingly digitalised world. India is going through a rapid digitisation, placing its banking sector in the middle of this revolution. The Banking sector, described as the “heart of all [systems]” by a participant of this study, is also the backbone of the critical information infrastructure of India. As a response to the increasing number of cyber threats, and the lack of nationally recognised and banked upon cyber resilience initiatives, this paper attempts to position cyber ranges as a policy capacity tool to further such initiatives, arguing for the viability of having an open-source dummy cyber range that is customisable. The study uses a multimethod qualitative approach to analyse the same, opting to interview experts and professionals, and draw comparative analysis of global frameworks to narrow down on relevant insights. It uses the Institutional Analysis Development Framework by Elinor Ostrom and Policy Analysis Capacity Framework by Michael Howlett. The study proposes a cyber range component blueprint for the BFSI sector, along with a broader cyber range framework for a cyber resilient critical information infrastructure of India.

title: Testing National Expansion Force: Japan's Curve and the Singapore-Dubai Mirror Cases

detail.abstract:
This paper undertakes the first case-based test of National Expansion Force (NEF), building on the theoretical boundaries established in the first paper and the measurement protocol developed in the second. Unlike the second paper, it does not place formulas, standardization procedures, or parameter rules at the center of the analysis. Instead, it uses calculated results as an evidentiary skeleton and examines Japan, Singapore, and Dubai/UAE as pilot cases to show what NEF can reveal beyond GDP, population, governance quality, and general competitiveness narratives.

Japan is the main case. Its distinctive feature is not low resources, weak industry, deficient infrastructure, or institutional collapse, but a form of high-level lock-in: material capacity and organizational order remain substantial, while the resource-to-cooperation conversion chain becomes sluggish and cannot reliably restart a new expansion cycle. Singapore and Dubai/UAE form a mirror pair. Singapore illustrates how a limited local capacity base can be amplified through institutionalized and deeply embedded cooperative structure. Dubai/UAE illustrates how limited local capacity can also be amplified through external capital, logistics, real estate, finance, and hub status, but with greater dependence on external conditions.

The paper compares NEF with GDP, GDP per capita, governance quality, and national-competitiveness-type indicators. Its purpose is not to reject existing indicators, but to show that they observe output, income, governance, or efficiency, while NEF asks whether these elements have been organized into a sustainable resource-cooperation conversion capacity. The cases demonstrate NEF’s differentiated explanatory value: Japan shows why high material capacity does not automatically generate expansion; Singapore shows why a small state can amplify stably; and Dubai/UAE shows why a hub can be powerful and fragile at the same time.

The paper remains a pilot test rather than a final empirical ranking. It preserves the constraints of the measurement protocol, treats the current calculations as reduced-form pilot results, and uses the cases to identify where the NEF framework can translate calculated curves into real-world interpretation. In particular, the 2007–2009 break in Japan is interpreted as pressure on the conversion chain under the pilot specification, not as a literal short-term collapse of cooperative structure itself.

title: The Impact of Job Autonomy on Employee Retention in the it Sector: A Comprehensive Analysis

title: Factors Influencing Employee Retention in the it Sector: A Comprehensive Review of Recognition, Compensation, Work Environment, and Job Autonomy

detail.title: Factors Influencing Employee Retention in the it Sector: A Comprehensive Review of Recognition, Compensation, Work Environment, and Job Autonomy
detail.abstract: Retention of employees is especially challenging in the aggressively competitive IT industry, and organizational success is heavily influenced by this factor. This thorough exploration considers the several factors that influence retention of employees, focusing on aspects like appreciation, remuneration, workplace, and independence at work. Drawing on theories such as the Job Characteristics Model, Self-Determination Theory, and Herzberg's Two-Factor Theory, the study incorporates findings from earlier research and common industry practice to give responses to what really matters. The review considers how non-monetary rewards, financial incentives, company culture, flexibility, and employees' control over their work influence them remaining with an organization. It also calls into question how the new work patterns of remote and hybrid working impact businesses, and how HR analytics, facilitated by AI, can shape retention practices. By pointing out current issues, setting out examples of best practice, and exploring future research areas, this report aims to provide actionable advice for business leaders and HR practitioners. The aim is to allow them to maintain a stable and loyal workforce within the IT sector, especially amidst ongoing talent shortages and changing employee expectations. The study recognizes the need for a balanced and responsive retention strategy, emphasizing job autonomy as a significant factor for employee satisfaction and commitment. In addition, strategic application of reward schemes, competitive pay levels, and benevolent working environments has a critical role to play.

title: Convexity and Short-termism in Banker Compensation
affiliations: Cornell University, SC Johnson Graduate School of Management, Department of Finance

detail.title: Convexity and Short-termism in Banker Compensation
detail.abstract: Two distinct mechanisms allow bank executives to personally profit from taking excessive risks: short-termism and convexity. While short-termism stems from timehorizon di erences between bank management and shareholders, convexity results from manager-shareholder alignment because bank stock is a highly leveraged optionlike bet on the bank's assets. Current U.S. policy initiatives intended to reduce risk taking do address short-termism but do not address convexity. I show how increased deferral periods, clawbacks, and penalties against bankers may backfire and increase the incentive to take risk if banks respond by granting even more of the convex stock units to management. Measures that would significantly reduce convexity-driven risk taking include replacing a portion of equity pay with concave instruments such as deferred forfeitable cash or contingent convertibles bonds, or increasing bank capital requirements.

title: Factor-Eliminating Technical Change, Human Capital Formation, and Development Traps
affiliations: Osaka Metropolitan University, Ehime University and Hiroshima University

detail.title: Factor-Eliminating Technical Change, Human Capital Formation, and Development Traps
detail.abstract: How does automation (factor-eliminating technical change) affect long-run development through its interaction with human capital formation? Although such technical change is often expected to promote growth, we show that it can instead slow or even halt capital accumulation. As automation displaces unskilled labor, the skill premium rises and induces education. Yet education responses are incomplete: partial skill upgrading expands the supply of skilled labor and limits further increases in skilled wages. Capital accumulation may therefore stall, trapping the economy in a low-capital steady state even when advanced technologies are available. We develop a general equilibrium model in which firms choose between production technologies and workers decide whether to acquire education. The model highlights a wage-stabilization mechanism through which endogenous technology adoption and human capital formation jointly shape wage dynamics and long-run development outcomes. When all workers become skilled, the economy converges to a high-capital equilibrium.

title: ENGAGEMENT OF STAKEHOLDERS IN CORPORATE SOCIAL RESPONSIBILITY IN THE MINING SECTOR: A LEGAL ANALYSIS

detail.title: ENGAGEMENT OF STAKEHOLDERS IN CORPORATE SOCIAL RESPONSIBILITY IN THE MINING SECTOR: A LEGAL ANALYSIS
detail.abstract: Stakeholder engagement is necessary to foster responsible mining practices that minimise negative environmental and social impacts. This study examined whether Tanzania’s CSR legal framework is effective in promoting meaningful stakeholder engagement in the mining sector. Doctrinal and comparative legal analyses were employed to evaluate the framework’s clarity, consistency and compliance with international standards. The findings highlight that Tanzania’s CSR legal framework has significant gaps and limitations, such as a lack of direct consultation with local communities, monitoring and evaluation mechanisms, consequences for non-compliance, criteria for priority determination, and the presence of statutory bureaucratic processes. These deficiencies impair not only effective stakeholder engagement but also compliance with international standards in supporting sustainable mining practices. Therefore, it is argued that, despite commendable legislative efforts by Tanzania to foster CSR stakeholder engagement, strategic legislative reforms are needed to promote responsible mining practices.

title: Soil-structure interaction influences the seismic resilience of mid-rise reinforced concrete structures located in soft-soil considering cumulative damage by weathering effects

detail.title: Soil-structure interaction influences the seismic resilience of mid-rise reinforced concrete structures located in soft-soil considering cumulative damage by weathering effects
detail.abstract: Soil–structure interaction (SSI) has been shown to significantly influence the seismic response of buildings, particularly for structures founded on soft soils. Because SSI effects depend on both soil properties and structural configuration, their impact is highly case-specific and must be evaluated for each particular scenario. Although SSI may reduce structural demands in some cases, it can also amplify seismic response, highlighting the need for detailed assessments. In addition, long-term deterioration processes such as weathering can progressively degrade structural properties, potentially affecting the seismic performance and recovery capacity of existing buildings.Over the past two decades, seismic resilience has emerged as a key concept in earthquake engineering, and numerous studies have proposed methodologies to quantify resilience and applied them to different structural typologies. However, the literature addressing resilience quantification while explicitly considering SSI effects remains limited. Even fewer studies incorporate the combined influence of SSI and structural deterioration due to weathering, leaving an important research gap.In this context, this study evaluates the seismic resilience of typical mid-rise reinforced concrete office buildings located on the soft soils of Mexico City, explicitly accounting for SSI, weathering effects, and cumulative damage. A resilience-based framework is implemented to quantify post-earthquake functionality and recovery. Results indicate that SSI tends to enhance seismic resilience by reducing structural demands, whereas weathering-induced deterioration significantly decreases the resilience index. These findings highlight the importance of incorporating both SSI and long-term deterioration effects in resilience assessments to achieve a more realistic representation of the post-earthquake recovery process of existing structures.

detail.abstract: Desertification is a major challenge to achieving the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals. The road network-based anti-desertification model (RNA-model), developed in the Horqin Sandy Land and widely applied in the Three-North Protective Forest Program, mitigates desertification through both direct structural effects and indirect effects that facilitate sand-control measures. However, their relative contributions and the minimum road construction intensity required for effective implementation remain unclear. Using eight periods of remote sensing data from 1990 to 2024, this study identified road-effect zones, quantified the contribution of the RNA-model to anti-desertification, and determined the minimum road kernel density threshold. Results showed that the total contribution of the road network to reducing desertified land area and severity ranged from 24.87% to 36.34%, with dominance shifting from indirect effects to balanced synergy with direct structural effects. A road kernel density threshold of 0.25 km km-2 was identified, supporting spatially differentiated management for land degradation mitigation.

title: BEYOND CONTENT: Cognitive Architecture as the Core Competency in the Age of Artificial Intelligence

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence has rendered content transmission obsolete as a primary educational objective. This paper argues that European educational systems must reorient toward the development of cognitive architecture-logic, judgment, metacognition, structured creativity-as the competency most structurally resistant to autonomous AI replication in the medium-to-long term. The urgency is empirically grounded: organizational AI adoption has reached 88% globally (Stanford HAI, 2026), while the expert-public gap on AI's labor impact stands at 50 percentage points-a structural signal of cognitive unpreparedness at population scale. The argument unfolds in five movements: the diagnosis of the structural obsolescence of contentcentered education; the identification of two forms of competency resistant to automation (embodied knowledge and structured cognitive architecture); the recovery of the classical tradition-with explicit reference to Dewey's reflective experience and Arendt's distinction between training and action-as empirical precedent for the teaching of structured thought; the proposal of the M-FUOCO-WECC framework as an operational pedagogical tool, including a direct refutation of the claim that corporate training can substitute cognitive formation; and the positioning of the proposal within the European context, anchored to the AI Act (2024) and Digital Education Action Plan 2021-2027, with a verifiable research agenda building on validated instruments including the California Critical Thinking Skills Test (CCTST). This paper is the second contribution of an organic theoretical series, in continuity with the sequential model Education → Cognition → Work → AI developed in the preceding paper (SSRN 6559358), deepening the analysis of the first node of that chain.

title: Interlocking Directorates, Innovation, and Knowledge Transmission

detail.title: Interlocking Directorates, Innovation, and Knowledge Transmission
detail.abstract: This paper quantifies how shared board members at competing companies affect innovation. To account for persistent differences in board member ability, I introduce AKM-estimated board member fixed effects as controls in the analysis of interlocks and innovation, using the connectedness of the board member-firm network to separate board member heterogeneity from firm heterogeneity. I show that board interlocks are associated with higher innovative output, which is matched by a parallel increase in cross-citations between the two interlocked partners. However, I provide suggestive evidence that these innovation dynamics are more consistent with strategic patenting or patent monitoring rather than genuine technological learning as the dominant mechanism. This is because the composition of those cross-citations does not tilt toward newly reached partner patents, newly reached technology classes, or technologically close inventions. Rather, the stronger responses are concentrated in citations to partner patents that are older, more prominent, and not technologically proximate to the citing patent.

title: CASE ANALYSIS REPORT-JCB in India

detail.abstract: This case analysis examines the strategic evolution of JCB’s international business forms in India from 1979 to the present, highlighting how regulatory environments and market conditions shape entry mode choices. In 1979, restrictive Indian foreign investment laws and high tariff barriers compelled JCB to enter the market through a 40-60 joint venture with Escorts Group. While the JV provided access to local market knowledge and risk sharing, it constrained JCB’s strategic control, limited technology transfer, and reduced investment incentives. Following India’s economic liberalization in the 1990s, JCB progressively acquired Escorts’ stake, converting the operation into a wholly owned subsidiary by 2002. Full ownership enabled JCB to protect proprietary technology, align Indian operations with global strategy, and scale manufacturing to meet infrastructure-driven demand. The shift illustrates key trade-offs between joint ventures and wholly owned subsidiaries: shared risk and local access versus control, IP protection, and integration. The analysis addresses strategic considerations in 1979 vs. 2005, the rationale for avoiding licensing, downsides of the JV structure, and the benefits and risks of complete control. JCB’s experience demonstrates how multinational corporations adapt entry strategies to institutional change, using phased ownership structures to balance market access with long-term competitive positioning. Ultimately, the transition underpinned JCB’s market leadership in India and strengthened its global standing against rivals such as Caterpillar, Komatsu, and Volvo CE.

title: United States Consumers’ Value Sustainable Critical Mineral Sourcing in Battery Electric Vehicles
affiliations: Missouri University of Science and Technology, Missouri University of Science and Technology and Missouri University of Science and Technology

detail.title: United States Consumers’ Value Sustainable Critical Mineral Sourcing in Battery Electric Vehicles
detail.abstract: Transportation sector contributes approximately 23% of U.S. greenhouse emissions and battery electric vehicles (BEVs) are a potential solution. BEV batteries are critical minerals intensive, yet scanty empirical evidence on how the mineral attributes of batteries influence consumer preferences. Utilizing a discrete choice experiment (DCE) with 600 U.S. consumers, we calculate willingness to pay (WTP) for four BEV battery mineral attributes: mineral intensity, domestic sourcing, reprocessed mineral content, and recyclability at end-of-life. Conditional and mixed logit models show significant consumer preferences for all attributes. WTP for a 1% increase in domestic sourcing is estimated at $66 and $70 for a 1% increase in battery recyclability, with a lower premium for recycled mineral content and a negative premium for mineral intensity. The mixed logit estimation shows considerable consumer preference heterogeneity. Our results imply that policies to localize and build recycling capacity have potential value for the BEV industry.

title: OCAF: A Gate-First Framework for Routine Macro-Financial and Supply-Chain Shock Assessment,JFS-facing merged manuscript v3 - abstract replacement, scoring transparency, decision-state table, and policy-utility patch

detail.title: OCAF: A Gate-First Framework for Routine Macro-Financial and Supply-Chain Shock Assessment,JFS-facing merged manuscript v3 - abstract replacement, scoring transparency, decision-state table, and policy-utility patch
detail.abstract: Routine macroeconomic and supply-chain releases often look safer than crisis events because their labels are familiar: CPI, payrolls, retail sales, purchasing-manager indices, freight disruptions, and commodity reports appear to invite immediate interpretation. This paper argues that this familiarity can create false certainty. We introduce the Output-Conditioned Authorization Framework (OCAF) as a gate-first macro-financial decision architecture that asks whether a routine-event judgment is authorized for release before producing a directional conclusion. OCAF assigns each event a PASS, RECON, or NO_OUTPUT state from a transparent M0-M8 scoring structure covering direction, regime stability, cross-market consistency, model uncertainty, and surprise. Using a 49-event universe and a structured supplementary event pool, the paper shows that many routine shocks should not be treated as clean forecasts: strong payroll and service-sector data may PASS, while CPI, manufacturing prices, retail sales, oil shocks, and central-bank paths often require RECON or NO_OUTPUT. Post-report validation from Hormuz, U.S. macro releases, and Japan policy data shows that the largest subsequent deviations concentrated in RECON or NO_OUTPUT variables rather than in clean PASS variables. OCAF is therefore not a point-forecasting model. It is a financial-stability release-governance framework for deciding when routine-event judgments are causally admissible, when they require conditional reconstruction, and when they should be withheld.

detail.abstract: This paper presents the Comprehensive Critical Thinking Framework (CCTF), a structured methodology for problem-solving and decision-making. The framework addresses two gaps in existing approaches. First, it includes assumptions, implications, stakeholder views, and implementation risks (AISI) as explicit, mandatory steps-not implied or left to user discretion. Second, it sequences steps in an order that prevents common analytical failures: criteria are defined before solutions are generated; evidence is gathered systematically per hypothesis or per option-criterion combination; and the AISI stress-test is applied after a preferred option emerges, not before. The paper describes two related frameworks-one for problem-solving, one for decision-making-unified by this structure.

detail.abstract: This paper studies the factors that lead to the success or failure of startup incubators in India. Despite hosting the third largest number of startups in the world, a huge percentage of these startups fail in the early stages of their inception. This is where incubators play a role as a bridge to support early-stage ventures by providing administrative and infrastructure requirements, along with mentorship. With policies of both state and central governments focusing on establishing new incubators, it is important to study the critical success factors. The research has been conducted using mixed methods, combining insights from secondary and primary research for analysis. Secondary research helped the student collect factors that affect startup incubation, and insights from primary research have helped list down the most important factors necessary for the growth of incubators and incubated startups in the country. A multistakeholder approach informs the study from multiple angles, including insights from stakeholders at the core, periphery and outside the incubator ecosystem to provide a holistic point of view for this study. In order to situate the Indian incubation ecosystem within a broader global context, the study also draws on comparative insights from the United Kingdom and Israel, which represent distinct models of innovation support through university-led clusters and risk-sharing incubation frameworks, respectively. Findings from the study suggest that while the government policies have focussed mainly on increasing the number of incubators across the country, their effectiveness and factors contributing to and limiting their effectiveness remain understudied. Homogenisation in the design and planning of incubators leads to standardised models that fail to address local needs and aspirations. There is also a lack of a feedback loop between incubators and government institutions supporting them, which limits the understanding of gaps and thus, the growth of the incubator itself. Additionally, the study finds that incubator relevance varies across business models, with service-based startups deriving less value from traditional incubation structures. This paper also provides policy-level solutions and proposes a conceptual model for continuous study of Incubator Effectiveness in India. These can be integrated into the system to increase the expanse and reach of the incubation system, cost-effective changes to the design and implementation, creating a feedback system for the incubation ecosystem and addressing fragmentation in the system.

title: Empirical Construction and Cross-Market Applications of a Global Fear & Greed Index (GFGI) and Sentiment Divergence Index (SDI): A Data-Driven Regime Discovery Framework

detail.title: Empirical Construction and Cross-Market Applications of a Global Fear & Greed Index (GFGI) and Sentiment Divergence Index (SDI): A Data-Driven Regime Discovery Framework
detail.abstract: Investor sentiment plays a fundamental role in asset price dynamics, yet existing composite measures-the CNN Fear & Greed Index for equities and the Crypto Fear & Greed Index for digital assets-operate in isolation, ignoring the crossmarket dynamics that have emerged as cryptocurrency and equity markets integrate. This paper makes two contributions. First, we construct a Global Fear & Greed Index (GFGI), formed as an inverse-volatility-weighted fusion of the two component indices (Qian, 2005; Maillard et al., 2010), and a Sentiment Divergence Index (SDI), which measures signed behavioural dislocation between markets. Second, we replace hand-drawn threshold-based regime tables with a data-driven pipeline: a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) on the joint (GFGI, SDI) space followed by a softmax classifier for real-time probabilistic regime assignment. Using daily data from February 2018 to December 2023, the GMM identifies six interpretable regimes. The Crypto-Led Greed regime produces a statistically significant mean 10-day BTC forward return of +6.69% (block-bootstrap 95% CI: [0.63%, 15.74%]). A dynamic allocation strategy achieves equivalent Sharpe ratio to a static 50/50 benchmark while improving the Sortino ratio by 5.1%, the Calmar ratio by 14.5%, and reducing maximum drawdown from-13.3% to-11.9%. The softmax classifier attains 94.2% out-of-sample accuracy. Granger causality tests, corrected for multiple testing via Benjamini-Hochberg, find no significant linear predictive relationship, suggesting SDI's value operates through non-linear regime identification. * The author thanks the open-source communities behind scikit-learn, statsmodels, and pandas for the computational tools used in this analysis. detail.abstract: This paper proposes a general framework for understanding value creation as a sequence of nonexpansive transformations of usable energy. Unlike traditional approaches that treat value and inputs as scalar quantities, this framework represents both as vectors and models value creation as a structured transformation process over time. Each transformation is defined as a linear operator subject to a non-expansiveness constraint, reflecting the irreversibility implied by thermodynamic principles. The framework decomposes transformations into spatial, structural, and value-reconfiguration components, providing a unified representation applicable across multiple scales.

title: From Prediction to Prioritization: Ranking Wells for Acid Stimulation using Data-Driven Methods
affiliations: Skolkovo Institute of Science and Technology, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Independent Researcher, Independent Researcher, Independent Researcher, Skolkovo Institute of Science and Technology and Skolkovo Institute of Science and Technology

detail.title: From Prediction to Prioritization: Ranking Wells for Acid Stimulation using Data-Driven Methods

keywords.keywords: Well TreatmentAcid stimulationPhysics-Guided graphs  Learn-to-Rank Foundation Oil\&Gas models

detail.abstract: The selection of wells for well‑treatment (WT) in oil and gas fields has traditionally relied on expert judgment and multi‑criteria decision analysis, which are subjective, labor‑intensive, and often yield suboptimal rankings. This paper proposes a data‑driven framework that ranks candidate wells for WT, specifically acid‑stimulation. To identify the best approach, we systematically compare three learning paradigms: (1) regression for point‑wise prediction of a continuous uplift value for each well independently; (2) classification for point‑wise prediction of a discrete effectiveness class; and (3) learn‑to‑rank for pairwise comparison of wells to directly optimize their relative ordering. The framework integrates physically grounded graphical models, which incorporate geological, technical, and inter‑well pressure‑maintenance factors with data-driven models, including tabular, time-series foundation models, and gradient boosting models. We evaluate the system on 3072 historical WT events and demonstrate a marked improvement in regression, classification and ranking over conventional baselines metrics. Specifically, the fine‑tuned time‑series foundation model performed best achieving a $R^2$ score of 0.87 for predicting the 6‑month mean uplift oil production rate, while the tabular foundation model attains a $ROC‑AUC$ of 0.84 for success determination, and the gradient boosting model reaches an $NDCG@10$ of 0.77 for ranking candidate well for WT. Using $NDCG@10$ as the unified evaluation metric, learn‑to‑rank clearly outperforms both regression and classification methods. Furthermore, an ablation study isolating the contribution of physics-based features revealed a significant performance gains across all evaluated metrics of at least 21\%. The approach delivers an objective decision-support tool that shortens planning, reduces bias, and improves treatment selection.

title: Dual-Scale Selective State-Space Model with Bidirectional Attentive Memory for Multi-Source Tool Wear Monitoring
affiliations: Ludong University, Dalian University of Technology, Ludong University, Ludong University, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Dalian University of Technology, University of Glasgow and Ludong University

detail.title: Dual-Scale Selective State-Space Model with Bidirectional Attentive Memory for Multi-Source Tool Wear Monitoring
detail.abstract: Accurate tool wear monitoring is crucial for the efficient and stable operation of smart manufacturing systems. However, multi-source sensor signals in complex cutting environments often couple high-frequency transient impacts with low-frequency long-term degradation trends. Traditional deep learning models, such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, frequently encounter challenges regarding long-range historical information decay and localized perceptual imbalance when processing such multi-scale features. To address these bottlenecks, this paper proposes a Bidirectional Long-term Attentive State Space Model (Bi-LASM). This model integrates bidirectional recurrent gating mechanisms with Selective State Space Models. Specifically, an adaptive multi-source signal fusion mechanism is designed to extract condition-sensitive channel features. Subsequently, an input-dependent dual-scale linear state space branch is constructed to decouple and parallelly fit the long-term smooth degradation patterns and short-term local mutation characteristics of the tool. Furthermore, a dynamic gating mechanism is introduced to achieve step-level adaptive weight allocation between long-term and short-term memory. Comprehensive experiments on an actual impeller milling dataset integrating force, vibration, sound pressure, and current sensors demonstrate that Bi-LASM achieves an overall recognition accuracy of 98.12%. This performance yields a 1.87% improvement over the pure Selective SSM baseline. Furthermore, the proposed model consistently outperforms mainstream architectures, including the Transformer and Bi-LSTM. The proposed method exhibits stable performance under complex working conditions and provides explicit physical interpretability for tool state evolution.

title: Assembling AI Regimes: Actor-Network Theory, National Problematisations, and the US-China-India Divergence
affiliations: Invespar Pte Ltd

detail.title: Assembling AI Regimes: Actor-Network Theory, National Problematisations, and the US-China-India Divergence
detail.abstract: This paper develops an Actor-Network Theory (ANT) framework for comparing emerging national artificial intelligence regimes in the United States, China, and India. It argues that the three regimes are being assembled around different actor-defined problematisations: full-stack dominance and rent capture in the United States; applicationsled industrial modernisation and strategic autonomy in China; and inclusive access through Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI) in India. Using the four moments of translation-problematisation, interessement, enrolment, and mobilisation-the paper traces the focal actors, non-human actants, attempted obligatory passage points, and inscriptions through which each network is being constituted. The comparison is symmetric: no case is treated as the baseline, contrast case, exception, or preferred model. The analysis further shows that the three actor-networks are interrelated. Export controls, compute dependencies, open-weight model ecosystems, cloud infrastructure, standards competition, foreign-platform enrolment, and public digital rails operate as inter-network actants that reshape the conditions under which each regime develops. The paper identifies differences in the scale of each attempted OPP, the fragilities of current mobilisation, and the implications of different value-capture configurations. It concludes that the United States, China, and India are not merely competing within a single AI race. They are assembling distinct socio-technical regimes for organising AI capability, access, infrastructure, and value.

title: European (EU) Capital Markets Law at (close to) 50: Historical Evolution and Missing Elements

detail.title: European (EU) Capital Markets Law at (close to) 50: Historical Evolution and Missing Elements

publicationDetails.detailsText: European Banking Institute Working Paper Series No. 207
publicationDetails.journalName: European Banking Institute (EBI) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
The purpose of this study is twofold: first, to briefly overview the evolution of European (EU) Capital Markets Law, from its origins in the late-1970ies until today, in the context of the currently developing Savings and Investment Union (SIU); and second, to identify missing elements, in particular in relation to the centralisation, at EU level, of supervisory tasks and powers in this sector of the EU financial system. It is structured in 6 Sections: 

Section A contains a definition of EU capital markets law and a brief overview of its evolution in four periods. The first three periods, until the outbreak of the Global Financial Crisis (GFC) in 2007, including both institutional and regulatory developments, are then discussed in Section B. The focus of the following three Sections C-E turns to the fourth period in the evolution of this branch of EU financial law: 

Section C overviews developments therein in the wake of the GFC, with specific emphasis on the establishment of the European System of Financial Supervision (ESFS) – including the European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA), as the institutional response to that crisis, and the further – and significant – enhancement of the regulatory framework;
Section D discusses the foundation of the Capital Markets Union (CMU), from the 2015 to the 2020 CMU Action Plans of the European Commission and their implementation, up to the retail investment strategy (RIS) and the 2024 “EU Listing Act”; and Section E develops on the current migration to the SIU, taking into account the proposals submitted (inter alia) in the 2024 Draghi Report, and then briefly presenting the key elements of the European Commission’s December 2025 market integration package (MIP).

Section F concludes with a brief assessment of the CMU project so far and of the ESMA’s direct supervisory powers, including a modest proposal towards further enhancing them beyond the legislative proposals included in the MIP.

Selected case-law of EU Courts is briefly discussed, as appropriate.

title: Beyond Infrastructure: Reimagining Civil Society’s Role in the UN Decade of Sustainable Transport and Strategic Pathways for Developing Contexts

detail.abstract:
This paper examines the structural architecture and strategic opportunities of the United Nations Decade of Sustainable Transport (2026-2035), with a focus on implications for social organizations in developing countries. Employing a critical policy analysis that integrates UN draft frameworks, comparative case studies, and contextual feasibility mapping, the study interrogates how civil society can transition from peripheral advocacy to co-implementation in sustainable mobility. 
Findings reveal that the Decade's enabling pillars-particularly data-driven governance, blended financing, and participatory planning-create unprecedented entry points for localized, community-led interventions. Contrary to conventional technocratic paradigms that prioritize capital-intensive infrastructure, this paper argues that grassroots organizations can deliver disproportionate impact by institutionalizing accessibility audits, open-data mobility platforms, and micropilot ecosystems. 
The Green Transformation and Sustainability Network (GXS) is positioned as a strategically aligned actor, leveraging its proposed Vietnam Pilot Hub to demonstrate scalable, low-capital models of people-centered urban mobility. The paper concludes with evidence-based recommendations for civil society engagement, challenging top-down financing assumptions and advocating for decentralized, equity-first transport governance.

title: Financial Panics in Open Economies
affiliations: Singapore Management University, Renmin University of China, Renmin University of China - School of Finance and University of International Business and Economics (UIBE) - School of Banking and Finance

detail.title: Financial Panics in Open Economies
detail.abstract: The external debt of emerging markets has seen a notable transition toward debt securities, which are typically uncollateralized and carry inherent run risk. We analyze financial vulnerability with unsecured debts by integrating financial panics à la Gertler et al. (2020) into an open economy model. In the model, capital inflows worsen the currency mismatch problems and increase the likelihood of runs by both domestic and foreign creditors, despite their stimulative effect on the real economy. The anticipation of financial panics can mitigate economic fluctuations caused by capital flows and provide new insights into stabilization policies. Capital controls and foreign exchange interventions (FXI) typically stabilize domestic economic activity when there are no anticipated financial panics, whereas they can, paradoxically, have destabilizing effects when financial panics are anticipated. Both policies can help reduce the frequency of panic runs and improve social welfare. Quantitatively, optimal policies generally feature near-zero probabilities of financial panics.

title: Emotional value triggered by social identification and personal fulfillment improves cooperation in spatial public goods games
affiliations: University of Shanghai for Science and Technology, University of Shanghai for Science and Technology and University of Shanghai for Science and Technology

detail.title: Emotional value triggered by social identification and personal fulfillment improves cooperation in spatial public goods games
detail.abstract: Game frameworks typically assume that agents pursue the maximization of objective material benefits, with emotional factors being treated merely as auxiliary behavioral variables. In this paper, we propose a novel public goods game framework where emotional value is directly incorporated into the fitness structure, serving as a tangible utility comparable to material payoff. In this mechanism, emotional value is determined according to the core and secondary functions, which are contingent upon the strategies employed by players and correlate with their social identification and personal fulfillment acquired within a specific memory window. Simulation results reveal that incorporation of emotional payoff in fitness function establishes a self-reinforcing feedback loop, where cooperators can attain a high level of social identification and fulfill elevated wealth expectations, thereby fostering the evolution of cooperation. Even in challenging game dilemmas where the enhancement factor is low, an optimal weighting of emotional value can counterbalance the material disadvantages of cooperation, enhancing stable clusters of cooperators that resist the invasion of defectors. Furthermore, extending memory length contributes to the sustainable development of cooperator clusters and leads to a state of complete cooperation across the entire range of enhancement factor. Particularly, the scaling of emotional perceptions exerts an important influence on cooperation, and the exponents in the derivation functions of emotional value play a crucial role in promoting cooperation.
